title: A Spectacular Planet Parade: Venus, Jupiter, and Mercury Align in June's Evening Sky
summary: Step outside after sunset this month and look west. You'll witness a rare celestial gathering: three planets—Venus, Jupiter, and Mercury—clustered together in the twilight sky. Even casual observers have likely noticed two brilliant 'stars' drawing closer each night. They are Venus and Jupiter, the two brightest planets visible to the naked eye. Venus outshines Jupiter by a factor of seven, gleaming with a silvery-white luster. On June 7, they'll stand side-by-side, separated by 2.3 degrees. By June 8, the gap shrinks to 1.8 degrees. The climax comes on June 9, when Venus slides just 1.6 degrees north of Jupiter—about three times the width of a full moon. Although their closest approach occurs during daylight hours for North America, they'll still appear strikingly near each other after sunset. After that, Jupiter will quickly drop toward the horizon and fade into twilight by early July. Venus, however, will remain high and brilliant, setting after 11 p.m. all month. Below this dazzling duo, you can spot Mercury, often called the 'elusive planet' because it never strays far from the sun. Right now, though, it's ideally placed for Northern Hemisphere viewers. About 45 minutes after sunset, locate Venus, then scan about 15 degrees down and to the right—roughly one and a half fist-widths at arm's length. Mercury shines at magnitude -0.2, as bright as the star Arcturus, with a subtle yellowish-orange hue. No telescope is needed, just a clear western horizon. This planetary parade is a perfect opportunity to connect with the cosmos, so mark your calendar and enjoy the show.
why_it_matters: Seeing multiple planets aligned gives a vivid, hands-on lesson in orbital mechanics and our place in the solar system; such events can spark a lifelong interest in astronomy and science, while also reminding us of the clockwork predictability of the cosmos.

background_read: Planetary conjunctions — when two or more planets appear close together in the sky — happen regularly because all planets orbit the Sun in roughly the same plane. Venus and Jupiter are the brightest planets visible from Earth; they have a cycle of conjunctions roughly every 13–14 months. Venus (the second planet from the Sun) is often called the evening or morning star, while Jupiter (the largest planet in our solar system) has dozens of moons and a powerful magnetic field. Mercury (the smallest planet and closest to the Sun) is notoriously hard to spot because it never ventures far from the Sun's glare, so opportunities like this are special. The star Arcturus (a bright orange giant in the constellation Boötes) is one of the brightest stars in the northern sky and serves as a convenient brightness benchmark. These three planets won't appear this close together again for several years, making June 2026 a rare window.

perspectives.description: This grouping is visible to anyone with a clear western view, no equipment needed. It offers a free, awe-inspiring experience that can draw families outside and ignite curiosity about the universe. For educators, it's a perfect real-world demo of planetary motion.

Light pollution from cities can wash out the view, and tall buildings or trees block the horizon. The peak alignment is brief; after June 9, Jupiter quickly disappears into twilight. Miss it, and you may wait years for a comparable show. Also, casual observers might confuse planets with airplanes or stars.

These conjunctions aren't actual close approaches — the planets are millions of kilometers apart, but their orbits bring them to the same line of sight. The geometry repeats predictably; the June 2026 event is simply a beautiful alignment of three bright objects. Studying these patterns helped ancient astronomers build early models of the solar system.

As Jupiter vanishes into solar glare by July, Venus remains a brilliant beacon until late evening through the month. Enthusiasts can track Venus and look forward to next conjunctions, perhaps involving Mars or Saturn. Digital sky maps and apps make it easier than ever to plan observations, encouraging long-term engagement with the night sky.
